title: Checking policies: distinguishing requests
objective: State "no cross-tenant read without an explicit share" as a query over all worlds, read each answer beside its witnesses, and say what a bounded check establishes.

blocks.md: Tests sample worlds. A solver can be asked about all of them.

choice.prompt: An agent reports: "On randomly generated small worlds, the new team-sharing rule never let anyone read another tenant's document without a share. Ship it." What has been established?

options.text: No world of any size has such a read.
options.why: Generated worlds sample a space; larger worlds stay open.

options.text: Such reads are absent from the worlds generated; checking every world is a different query.
options.why: This is a test over n worlds, stamped [T], and no more.

options.text: Nothing, unless a request shows where the old and new rules differ.
options.why: That overcorrects: the tests establish something, and no more.

blocks.md: Hunt for a violation by asserting its negation, as in S1: some user reads a document of another tenant, and no share to the user or the user's teams explains it. Here `sat` is a distinguishing world. `unsat` counts only beside two witnesses: the premises hold together, and some read is allowed at all, because a policy that denies everything satisfies every confidentiality property.

blocks.direction: Query asserts: a cross-tenant read with no explicit share, under the policy alone. `sat` means such a world exists.

code.text:
from z3 import *

User, Team, Doc, Tenant = [DeclareSort(n) for n in ("User", "Team", "Doc", "Tenant")]
member     = Function("member", User, Team, BoolSort())
owns       = Function("owns", Team, Doc, BoolSort())
share_user = Function("share_user", Doc, User, BoolSort())
share_team = Function("share_team", Doc, Team, BoolSort())
revoked    = Function("revoked", Doc, User, BoolSort())
tenant_u   = Function("tenant_u", User, Tenant)   # a user's tenant
tenant_t   = Function("tenant_t", Team, Tenant)   # a team's tenant, and so its documents'

u, d, t1, t2 = Const("u", User), Const("d", Doc), Const("t1", Team), Const("t2", Team)

rule1 = And(member(u, t1), owns(t1, d))             # a member of the owning team t1
rule2 = And(share_user(d, u), Not(revoked(d, u)))   # shared with the user, not revoked
rule3 = And(member(u, t2), share_team(d, t2))       # shared with one of the user's teams
canread = Or(rule1, rule2, rule3)

# the violation: a read across tenants that no explicit share explains
violation = And(canread, Not(rule2), Not(rule3), tenant_u(u) != tenant_t(t1))

# WF1: a member belongs to the team's tenant
x, y = Const("x", User), Const("y", Team)
wf1 = ForAll([x, y], Implies(member(x, y), tenant_u(x) == tenant_t(y)))

def verdict(*facts):
    s = Solver()
    s.set("rlimit", 1000000)
    s.add(*facts)
    return s.check()

print("no invariants :", verdict(violation))
# after your call, remove the # marks and run again
# print("with WF1      :", verdict(violation, wf1))
# print("premises      :", verdict(wf1, canread))   # the premises hold together
# print("non-vacuity   :", verdict(wf1, rule1))     # some read is allowed at all

tap.property: no user reads another tenant's document without an explicit share

call.prompt: The query has no schema invariants yet. What will Z3 return?

options.text: `sat`
options.why: A Birch user on an Acme team reads an Acme document with no share.

options.text: `unsat`
options.why: Nothing yet keeps a membership inside its tenant.

options.text: `unknown`
options.why: No quantifier ranges over a hierarchy yet, so Z3 decides it.

blocks.after: Z3 returns `sat` {{run:RUN-z3-cross-tenant}}: nothing keeps a membership inside its tenant, so a Birch user on an Acme team can read an Acme document unshared. Remove the `#` marks and run again: with WF1, that a member belongs to the team's tenant, the violation is gone, beside two satisfiable witnesses.

blocks.md: Teams nest, so a member belongs to every ancestor team too. Cedar's paper (section 4.3) describes three ways to give a solver that. Leave the hierarchy unconstrained, which admits a spurious violation that needs a cycle. State acyclicity and transitivity as quantified rules, which can make the encoding undecidable. Or ground the hierarchy as data and constrain only the teams the query mentions, its footprint.

blocks.direction: Query asserts: a user reaches a team of another tenant by membership or nesting. The cell prints a verdict for each encoding.

code.text:
from z3 import *

User, Team, Doc, Tenant = [DeclareSort(n) for n in ("User", "Team", "Doc", "Tenant")]
member   = Function("member", User, Team, BoolSort())
subteam  = Function("subteam", Team, Team, BoolSort())   # subteam(s, t): s is nested directly in t
nested   = Function("nested", Team, Team, BoolSort())    # nested at any depth
mid      = Function("mid", Team, Team, Team)             # a team between s and t
owns     = Function("owns", Team, Doc, BoolSort())
tenant_u = Function("tenant_u", User, Tenant)
tenant_t = Function("tenant_t", Team, Tenant)

u, x = Consts("u x", User)
s, m, t = Consts("s m t", Team)
d = Const("d", Doc)

wf1 = ForAll([x, t], Implies(member(x, t), tenant_u(x) == tenant_t(t)))
wf2 = ForAll([s, t], Implies(subteam(s, t), tenant_t(s) == tenant_t(t)))

# nested is the transitive closure of subteam, written as quantified rules
closure = [
    ForAll([s, t], Implies(subteam(s, t), nested(s, t))),
    ForAll([s, m, t], Implies(And(nested(s, m), nested(m, t)), nested(s, t))),
    ForAll([s, t], Implies(nested(s, t), Or(subteam(s, t), And(nested(s, mid(s, t)), nested(mid(s, t), t))))),
]
acyclic = ForAll([t], Not(nested(t, t)))                 # WF3: no team nests in itself

# the violation: u reaches team t by membership or nesting, t owns d, and the tenants differ
reach = Or(member(u, t), Exists([s], And(member(u, s), nested(s, t))))
violation = And(reach, owns(t, d), tenant_u(u) != tenant_t(t))

def verdict(*facts):
    sv = Solver()
    sv.set("rlimit", 1000000)
    sv.add(*facts)
    r = sv.check()
    return str(r) + (" (" + sv.reason_unknown() + ")" if r == unknown else "")

print("unconstrained:", verdict(wf1, wf2, *closure, violation))
print("quantified   :", verdict(wf1, wf2, *closure, acyclic, violation))

# grounded: the hierarchy is data. Only the teams the query mentions get constraints,
# and nesting runs two levels deep.
T = [Const("t%d" % i, Team) for i in range(3)]
def in_team(user, team):
    return Or(member(user, team),
              *[And(member(user, a), subteam(a, team)) for a in T],
              *[And(member(user, a), subteam(a, b), subteam(b, team)) for a in T for b in T])
g_wf1 = And(*[Implies(member(u, a), tenant_u(u) == tenant_t(a)) for a in T])
g_wf2 = And(*[Implies(subteam(a, b), tenant_t(a) == tenant_t(b)) for a in T for b in T])
g_violation = Or(*[And(in_team(u, a), owns(a, d), tenant_u(u) != tenant_t(a)) for a in T])
print("grounded     :", verdict(g_wf1, g_wf2, g_violation))

call.prompt: What will Z3 return for the quantified encoding?

options.text: `sat`
options.why: A quantified query need not give a definite answer.

options.text: `unsat`
options.why: Z3 cannot show that without induction, and no counterexample is no proof.

options.text: `unknown`, with its reason
options.why: There is no verdict, so a guarded change fails closed.

blocks.after: Z3 stops without a verdict and says why, here `unknown (push canceled)` {{run:RUN-z3-hierarchy-unknown}}. A guard fails closed on that, as Amazon's Block Public Access analysis does on a time-out ([ESEC/FSE 2020](https://doi.org/10.1145/3368089.3409728)). The grounded encoding decides, because the hierarchy is data, and WF2 and WF3 become facts you validate about each world.

choice.prompt: Which definition of `explicit(u, d)` matches the policy?

options.text: `(share_user(d, u) ∧ ¬revoked(d, u)) ∨ (∃t. member(u, t) ∧ share_team(d, t))`
options.why: It mirrors rules 2 and 3.

options.text: `share_user(d, u) ∨ (∃t. member(u, t) ∧ share_team(d, t))`
options.why: It drops the revocation.

options.text: `(share_user(d, u) ∧ ¬revoked(d, u)) ∨ (∀t. member(u, t) → share_team(d, t))`
options.why: Subset where overlap was meant, vacuously true for a user on no team.

blocks.md: A bounded check lists every world inside a stated scope and runs the policy on each. Jackson's small scope hypothesis says that many bugs have small counterexamples, so it finds many of them. The scope here is eight worlds: two teams, two tenants, one user, one document, and the user's team nested in the document's team or not.

blocks.direction: Query asks: which worlds have a cross-tenant read (`violation`), and which break WF2 (`wf2_broken`)?

code.text:
.decl world(w: symbol, a1: symbol, a2: symbol, nested: symbol)
.decl tenant_of_team(w: symbol, t: symbol, a: symbol)
.decl tenant_of_user(w: symbol, u: symbol, a: symbol)
.decl member(w: symbol, u: symbol, t: symbol)
.decl owns(w: symbol, t: symbol, d: symbol)
.decl subteam(w: symbol, s: symbol, t: symbol)
.decl inteam(w: symbol, u: symbol, t: symbol)
.decl canread(w: symbol, u: symbol, d: symbol)
.decl violation(w: symbol)
.decl wf2_broken(w: symbol)
.output violation
.output wf2_broken

// the scope: two teams, two tenants, one user in t1, one document owned by t2,
// and t1 nested in t2 or not. Every such world is one row.
world("w1", "acme", "acme", "no").    world("w2", "acme", "acme", "yes").
world("w3", "acme", "birch", "no").   world("w4", "acme", "birch", "yes").
world("w5", "birch", "acme", "no").   world("w6", "birch", "acme", "yes").
world("w7", "birch", "birch", "no").  world("w8", "birch", "birch", "yes").

// each world's facts
tenant_of_team(w, "t1", a) :- world(w, a, _, _).
tenant_of_team(w, "t2", a) :- world(w, _, a, _).
tenant_of_user(w, "u", a) :- world(w, a, _, _).
member(w, "u", "t1") :- world(w, _, _, _).
owns(w, "t2", "d") :- world(w, _, _, _).
subteam(w, "t1", "t2") :- world(w, _, _, "yes").

// the policy: rule 1 with nesting (the worlds hold no shares)
inteam(w, u, t) :- member(w, u, t).
inteam(w, u, t) :- inteam(w, u, s), subteam(w, s, t).
canread(w, u, d) :- inteam(w, u, t), owns(w, t, d).

// a violation: a read across tenants
violation(w) :- canread(w, u, d), tenant_of_user(w, u, a), owns(w, t, d), tenant_of_team(w, t, b), a != b.
// WF2: a subteam belongs to its parent's tenant
wf2_broken(w) :- subteam(w, s, t), tenant_of_team(w, s, a), tenant_of_team(w, t, b), a != b.

call.prompt: Every violating world also breaks WF2, so with WF2 there is no violation within the scope. Which stamp does that earn?

options.text: [M] · scope · complete within the scope
options.why: Every world inside the bound was checked, and none beyond it.

options.text: [P] for every world
options.why: The small scope hypothesis says where bugs usually live; it is not a theorem.

blocks.after: Eight worlds is the whole scope; a third team, a share or deeper nesting lies outside it. Jackson (York, 2004-02-04, slides 18 and 19) puts it this way: bounded analysis is sound, with no false alarms, but incomplete. Drawer D-16 shows the same in Alloy.

choice.prompt: A check lists every world within a stated scope and finds no violation. Which statement is true?

options.text: No world of any size violates the policy.
options.why: Worlds beyond the scope were never examined.

options.text: No world within the scope violates it, and a larger world might.
options.why: The check is complete within its bound and silent beyond it.

options.text: Nothing is established, because a bounded check is only a test.
options.why: Inside its scope the enumeration is exhaustive, not a sample.

choice.prompt: Which result is paired with the stamp it earns?

options.text: A matrix on one world with no cross-tenant cell: [T] · 1 world.
options.why: It tests a single world and says nothing about any other.

options.text: A bounded enumeration with no violation: [P] for every world.
options.why: It is complete within its scope only, so its stamp names the scope.

options.text: An `unsat` with neither witness: [P] · Z3 unsat · uncertified.
options.why: A policy that denies everything is `unsat` too.

options.text: An `unknown`: [T], no violation found.
options.why: `unknown` earns [?], and a guarded change fails closed.

blocks.title: Twin
blocks.md: Cedar's second layer is a per-change symbolic analysis: a new policy set is equivalent to, more or less permissive than, or incomparable with the old one, shown by a distinguishing request. AWS IAM Access Analyzer's `CheckNoNewAccess` asks the same question. Pins: {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}.

A pin is the commit a ref pointed to when ls-remote read it; read_at is that instant. The record is stale 60 days after its started_at and is refreshed by re-running the commands in argv.

git ls-remote was first run with several ref patterns per command (HEAD plus refs/tags/... or refs/heads/...); for leanprover/lean4 and postgres/postgres that printed nothing with exit 0. The recorded run uses one pattern per command; the pin for lean4 tags and PR 14577 uses a trailing * pattern, and every matching ref is kept in refs.

refs/pull/14577/merge is not advertised; only refs/pull/14577/head is. The v4.35.0 tag points at eb6cafb7290e8bd5f2937522d8d804f58f02bafc, the commit the bench image's Lean prints in its version string.

Twin cards that name no git repository are not pinned here: Stripe's "Idempotent requests" API page, the Zanzibar paper (USENIX ATC 2019), Jepsen's PostgreSQL 12.3 analysis, the arXiv papers on Cedar and CCF, SymCert (FMCAD 2026) and the AWS Automated Reasoning checks pages. Each card states its own read date.
